section: Full 1977-2014 detail cut from the main narrative
text:
Full 1977-2014 detail cut from the main narrative
The three subperiods (grounded in the digitized UCLA General Catalogs 2003–05 through 2013–14; Sears’s dates independently confirmed):

ISSR proper, 1977 – late 2000s. An OECD international directory dates the “ISSR Data Archive at UCLA” to December 1977, for quantitative research “primarily secondary analysis,” drawing on UCLA’s ICPSR membership plus federal statistical agencies (Census, NCHS, NCES, BLS) and local studies like LACSS.
Institute for Social Research (ISR), ~2009–2011. Parent institute renamed by the 2009–10 UCLA General Catalog, same phone, same components including the Data Archive, new website (isr.ucla.edu). Still in the 2010–11 catalog. No director identified under this name.
Standalone SSDA, ~2011–2014. By the 2011–12 catalog neither ISSR nor ISR appears; SSDA is listed independently as a Social Sciences collection with its own site (dataarchives.ss.ucla.edu). No public source names a formal dissolution of the parent or a single successor. The reporting line from here to the 2014 Library transfer is unresolved.
Immediately pre-transfer (2013), SSDA was piloting the DDI-Lifecycle metadata standard and Colectica curation software.
Southern California Social Survey (SCSS), confirmed running 1984-1991 in the Harvard Dataverse SSDA collection (true start year not pinned down, likely closer to 1977-1980, never deposited in ICPSR at all).
1988 technical infrastructure detail: mainframe (IBM 3090, MVS/VM-CMS), tape management (DTA/DTB numbering system), UCLA’s ORION catalog, ICPSR’s SPIRES search facility, a microcomputer-based (dBase III) tape-tracking system Pawlocki and Stephenson built.1
Rotating annual LACSS PIs: Lawrence Bobo (1992, then UCLA Assoc. Professor of Sociology).
Cross-national work in more depth: the Intergenerational Stratification and Mobility File (ISMF), built with Harry Ganzeboom (Free University, Amsterdam) and Donald Treiman, funded by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO), Project H50.293.2

Sources: Pawlocki and Stephenson (1988); ICPSR’s catalog records for the LAMAS, SCSS, and LACSS series; Stiles and Stephenson (2008).

text:
Full Doug Daniels project inventory
Drawn from Daniels’s project records, press coverage, and award records, and from DSC’s annual data summaries. Highlights not in the main narrative:

Easter Island Moai statuette scanning (Jan-March 2022) with Jo Anne Van Tilburg (Director, Rock Art Archive, Cotsen Institute), accepted as Chapter 9, “Moai Anatomy and Ahu Sequence,” in Te Moai Rapa Nui: The Statues of Easter Island: An Illustrated Atlas (Cotsen Institute of Archaeology Press, ~500pp, expected ~early 2025).
Stein Eye Institute conjunctiva-tissue scanning (Spring 2022); Anatomy Lab cadaver-arm scanning with Dr. Anthony Friscia and Prof. Chien-Ling Liu Zeleny (Fall 2022), now used in History of Medicine coursework.
Drone/LiDAR mapping kit acquired late spring/early summer 2023; FAA Part 107 UAS Remote Pilot certification. Used on an ongoing Angkor Wat temple-mapping project (Cambodia/Philippines) and the Mosfell Valley, Iceland survey, one trip, Summer–Fall 2024 (per Tim 2026-09-02; an earlier “summer 2023” mention was planning).
LiDAR-scanned Powell Library twice: terrestrial LiDAR, Nov-Dec 2021 (“for preservation, documentation, and exhibition of 3D data tools”), and drone-based photogrammetry/aerial mapping, Summer 2024.
Vietnamese Heritage Museum cultural-heritage scanning (Spring-Summer 2024), alongside the separately-documented “Little Saigon @ UCLA: International Digital Archaeology Day” (with UCLA classics professor Kelly Nguyen, 50+ high school students, 30 community members).
Department of Medicine (Endocrinology/Pathology) biological-specimen scanning for thyroid research, Nov-Dec 2025.
A 3D-printed surgical probe holder (with an undergraduate student), now used at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center.
Recurring Powell Society donor open-house demos, March 2017/2018/2019, a direct link between Doug’s work and Norman Powell’s ongoing patronage relationship.
Professional service: Liberal Technology Group (founding member, 2020-present); CS3DP, Community Standards for 3D Preservation (member, 2018-present, IMLS-funded); UC 3D Data Common Knowledge Group (member since 2020, chair since 2024); IIIF 3D Community Group (member since 2022, co-chair since 2024); UC Love Data Week (UCLA campus liaison, 2024).

UCLA Law Behind Bars Data Project (COVID-19 in prisons, jails, youth facilities, immigration detention), Dataverse collection created 2022-01-28, 1,169 items. Project itself run by UCLA Law; no explicit DSC credit on the project’s own homepage, though the Dataverse collection is real and dated.
Williams Institute (LGBT law and policy research), Dataverse collection created 2021-05-27, small footprint (3 items) but DSC’s curation/consulting work supported Williams Institute data reaching ICPSR directly: TransPop (ICPSR 37938, first national probability sample of transgender individuals in the US; co-investigators Walter Bockting, Columbia; Jody Herman, UCLA; Sari Reisner, Harvard/Fenway), Generations (ICPSR 37166, five-year longitudinal LGB health study), the combined Generations/TransPop dataset (ICPSR 38421), and Mapping LGBTQ Equality: 2010 to 2020 (ICPSR 37877).
Cotsen Institute of Archaeology (108 items) and DIG, Digital Information Gateway (6,360 items), both Dataverse collections created 2020-09-16. DIG’s stated mission: “expand citation practices” in archaeology.

Sources: the collections’ public UCLA Dataverse pages and DSC project records.

text:
Full visualization methodology
Survey-year bar chart (titled “Survey years represented in the surviving SSDA collection” since 2026-09-27; earlier drafts called it “holdings activity,” which overstated what it shows): 571 datasets in the Harvard Dataverse SSDA collection (dataverse.harvard.edu/dataverse/ssda_ucla), pulled via the collection’s search API 2026-08-09, bucketed by the survey year embedded in each dataset’s title (regex-matched, last 4-digit year 1930-2026 in the title string), not the Dataverse “published” date (uniformly 2015-2018, a migration artifact). This is a distinct, smaller number from the “1,014 legacy Social Science Data Archive datasets” Tim’s own Data Summary says were harvested into UCLA’s own live Dataverse instance, different scope (Harvard-hosted historical sub-collection vs. UCLA’s current live instance), don’t conflate the two counts.
Citation search: queried live via browser automation against ICPSR’s per-study “Data-related Publications” search (icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/search/publications?q=STUDY_NO:{n}), 2026-08-09, this endpoint is Cloudflare-blocked to scripted/curl access (confirmed, HTTP 403), which is why browser automation was needed. Checked: all 5 confirmed LACSS study records (36599, 36600, 36598, 36563, 36749) and all 8 confirmed LAMAS waves (36631, 36612, 36611, 36624, 36615, 36614, 36607, 36617). SCSS was searched separately for its own ICPSR presence and found to have none: it was not deposited at ICPSR, confirmed via a direct ICPSR search for “Southern California Social Survey” (only the 5 LACSS records matched, as background-text mentions, not actual SCSS deposits). So this search cannot measure SCSS. The 1991 SCSS is on Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/JH9UXH), and a 2023 article analyzes it (see the main text).
Sources: ICPSR’s Bibliography of Data-related Literature, searched by study number (August 2026), and ICPSR’s catalog records for the series.

title: Research companion: full evidence for the SSDA/DSC institutional history
text:
Full 2018–2026 account
The longer version of the 2018–2026 chapter, moved here from the main history on 2026-09-27 when that chapter was reorganized around four cases. It is kept intact (apart from corrected 3D-scan credit and editorial notes moved to Open questions), so it overlaps the main text in places. Hosted collections, the Daniels inventory, and the Powell gifts have their own sections elsewhere in this companion.
This is the era with the widest gap between the unit’s size and its reach, and the era this history’s author directed. It is written against institutional records and cited sources rather than recollection, and the judgments in it are marked as judgments. The full evidence trail is in this companion and the author’s private working notes.

Continuity, not rupture
The 2018 rebrand changed the unit’s name and widened its scope. It did not replace what came before. ucla-data-archive_old, a repository built around the “Data Archive” identity, holding its collections policies, terms, and deposit and preservation practices, was created in July 2017 and actively maintained through May 2020, two years after the unit’s formal name became “Data Science Center.” The archive’s core work, repository hosting, which descends directly from the LAMAS, SCSS, and LACSS series, ran under the new name the whole time. Jina “Jamie” Jamison, who came across with the archive in 2014, still leads that repository work today. She is the one human through-line across the whole Library era.
The growth over that span is easy to state. Staff went from 2.0 FTE at the 2014 transfer (a director and a data archivist) to five by about 2021, mostly by redesigning existing library positions rather than hiring new ones: a geospatial librarian moved in from another department and was rebuilt as a Spatial Data Science Librarian (Zhiyuan Yao), a data manager from the Library’s IT division was rebuilt as a Data Science Facilitator, and a Digital Library programmer with a machine-learning background was recruited across divisions (Kristian Allen, a 0.5-FTE role, 2018–2024).3 Datasets deposited directly in UCLA Dataverse went from 9 in January 2020 to about 376 by February 2026, and downloads across the repository rose from 229 to more than 143,000.4 The staffing did not grow in proportion. Part of how the unit absorbed the load is the student program described below; part is that some capacity was simply lost, a GIS position left unfilled after August 2024 and not refilled, and other roles ended, with the demand in those areas still there.


What stayed constant, and what changed
For six decades and five institutional homes the constant has been the same: keep research evidence findable, usable, and preserved, and extend that to whatever kind of evidence researchers happened to be producing. What changed after 2018 is the range of things that covers. Not only survey datasets now, but restricted and sensitive data that needs governed computation, geospatial data and aerial imagery, 3D and spatial capture, text corpora and computational text analysis, research software, and course material treated as a citable output.5 Look back at that list and it tracks the field’s own sequence, from data citation to open and FAIR data to open science to software curation to computationally intensive research support. That is a way of narrating what changed after the fact, not a plan anyone was working to. The sections below take the main strands one at a time.


The repository: UCLA Dataverse
The legacy SSDA collection had lived on Harvard’s hosted Dataverse. In 2018 the DSC stood up a local UCLA instance, chosen for the same reasons the archive had chosen Dataverse in the first place: DDI metadata, the ability to restrict licensed data, and a curation ladder from self-service deposit to fully mediated. The DSC wired it to UCLA single sign-on, DOI minting, and preservation through the California Digital Library. Research groups run their own branded sub-collections inside it with DSC training, and the Library uses it to manage discovery and access for data it buys.6 One deliberate choice was to harvest the legacy SSDA collection into the discovery layer rather than migrate it right away: keep it working first, move it later.
Growth came in three steps. Late 2021 was the institutional scale-up, when schools and centers began running their own collections. Mid to late 2022 brought the legacy SSDA holdings into the local discovery layer, along with wider campus adoption. From 2023 on the growth was steady. By January 2026 the repository had 135 collections (92 published), 312 user accounts, and about 54,700 released files. The day-to-day work was Jamie Jamison’s. She wrote the preservation documentation, represented UCLA at the 2021 Dataverse Community Meeting, and kept the continuity guarantees working: automated nightly database dumps to cloud storage, consolidated storage buckets, current certificates, and a tested scripted install so the system could be rebuilt if it had to be. She walked depositors through sub-collections, DOIs, and archiving, handled access to the LARIAC imagery, and when Redivis arrived became the first approver for restricted-data requests. She is named as data manager on the published L2 voter dataset.
The collections DSC hosts now run well past social science. The UCLA Law Behind Bars Data Project covers COVID-19 in prisons, jails, and detention nationally, about 1,169 items. The Williams Institute’s LGBT law-and-policy data, which DSC curation helped bring to ICPSR directly, includes TransPop, the first national probability sample of transgender people in the US. The DIG archaeology collection alone lists about 6,360 items in its Dataverse search results (a count that can mix datasets, files, and sub-collections, so it is not comparable with the SSDA dataset counts). DIG’s own stated aim, to “expand citation practices” in archaeology, is the same bibliographic-control instinct Stephenson brought to the 1980s, applied to a different field at a much larger scale.
Reuse is harder to count than deposits. In one indexing pass (system, date, and exclusions still to be confirmed), 180 of about 959 datasets carried a link to a publication, and 13 of those papers can be traced in OpenAlex, with 258 citations between them. That is a floor, not an estimate. A DataCite export bug drops links, restricted and draft datasets are left out, archaeology datasets tied to books have no DOI to follow, and about 200 public datasets have no publication link on file. The traceable depositors include a radiation-belt modeling group in Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences led by Yuri Shprits that deposits again and again (four linked papers, 95 citations).
Running a repository also meant defending it. In early 2025, bots mass-downloaded UCLA Dataverse content, apparently to train a model, rotating across thousands of addresses to get around IP blocking, from about April to July. Tim identified an open-source bot filter, Anubis, as the fix, and Jamison put it into production and tuned it, with host-level blocking alongside, so that abusive traffic was stopped without locking out researchers. The attack was contained by summer with no loss to the collection.7


Consulting: from reference desk to research partner
The archive had always answered questions: data discovery, codebook lookups, help with SPSS, SAS, and Stata. The 2018 redesign kept that and widened it. The DSC’s new mission statement, written through a design-thinking exercise that put the scholar at the center, named the whole research life cycle: planning and data management plans, acquisition, storage, cleaning, analysis, publication, curation, and preservation.8 In practice that meant consultations on data cleaning, visualization, coding, and methods such as text and cluster analysis. As the team’s skills grew it added GIS, 3D and drone capture, machine learning, research software, reproducible workflows, and open-source licensing.
Not all of it happened one-on-one. The team ran Tidy Tuesday, a weekly social data-cleaning lab; judged an inaugural datathon with an Anderson student group in spring 2020; and helped program a UC-wide Love Data Week of more than 25 workshops and events. It taught inside degree programs too: the Sustainable LA Grand Challenge undergraduate scholars, the Mellon Mays fellows, and graduate programs in social science, urban planning, applied statistics, and management.9
The volume is documented for the later years. From 2023 through 2025 DSC recorded 785 scheduled consultations, 156 service-desk tickets, and 234 tracked project collaborations. The categories describe different kinds of work and should be read separately. The School of Public Affairs, the Social Sciences division, and Life Sciences brought the most consultations. Over the same years the work changed shape, from single appointments toward project support that ran for months, and the longest of those engagements are in Research impact.10


Governed computation: Redivis and the L2 voter file
Before this, UCLA had no campus service for restricted data of this class outside Mednet, the medical enterprise’s computing environment (with HIPAA-level services such as a HIPAA-compliant Box), which the rest of campus could not use. There was no governed way to give a student access to a voter file, and no secure place outside medicine to merge FERPA-, PII-, or PHI-restricted data at scale (author’s account, 2026-09-27). To support that class of data, DSC selected and licensed Redivis, ran the institutional compliance review (Third-Party Risk Management, P3/P4 approval), negotiated access to the restricted datasets, piloted the platform in 2022, and launched the governed service in January 2023. It set up a 50-seat model with data-use-agreement controls so that routine requests would not pile up on one person.11
The main case is the L2 historic voter file, more than 10 TB of national voter history bought through the archive’s gift fund. It arrived as thousands of fragmented state-level files, too large to store locally and too inconsistent to analyze. DSC pulled it into a single version-controlled national dataset, published with its own DOI (UCLA Library, L2 Voter History and Demographic Dataset, 2023, doi:10.60603/D37P4R) and presented at FORCE11 2024 by Redivis’s CEO alongside the doctoral student who curated it, Graham Straus. Straus put the institutional point plainly: “What happens when I leave UCLA? Will people know how the dataset was constructed? Yes!” Researchers use it directly across departments, in election administration, gentrification, Latino voting, and a project merging the voter file with UCLA medical records to study health and voting. Recorded processing on the platform grew from 444 GB in its first year to 2.9 PB in 2024; those figures measure platform activity, not data held (holdings are about 20 TB). DSC provided the environment and the access. The scholarship stayed with the researchers. The point of it is not an “AI” story. It is that stewardship came to include governed computation, not only acquiring and describing open files.


Infrastructure: running it in the cloud
Almost none of this ran on hardware DSC owned. UCLA Dataverse runs on Amazon Web Services, with its files in S3, about 5.4 TiB counting replication as of May 2025. The point-cloud service described below runs on its own AWS server with about 4.5 TiB of storage, shared with the LARIAC imagery. Redivis is a licensed platform, not a local system. The exceptions were a deep-learning workstation in the Young Research Library, bought with a Powell gift; the 3D workstation and drone kit; and an R server DSC hosted for research groups whose data outgrew their own machines, Carceral Ecologies among them.
Paying for it involved two funds with different jobs. Dataverse first ran under an AWS account belonging to the Library’s IT division. When campus broke up its shared AWS arrangement and DSC got its own account, the cost landed on DSC; Powell infrastructure funds covered it for about two years, and then it came out of the archive’s operating fund, the one the 2014 transfer set up. That fund paid the recurring costs: ICPSR and Roper (both moved to higher pricing tiers over time), AWS, and Redivis after two years of University Librarian discretionary backing. SDA and Colectica were dropped. The Library added money to the fund over time to cover the growth. The gift fund, the Data Archive Purchase Fund (fund no. 604970/56972), bought data instead: the L2 voter file, the LARIAC imagery, and four licensed English corpora (COCA, COHA, NOW, and the Coronavirus Corpus) held in UCLA Dataverse for UCLA faculty and graduate students.12
Keeping the systems current was its own work. By 2025 production ran Dataverse 5.14, a release line upstream no longer patches, and DSC had begun rebuilding the service as code: Terraform for the AWS resources, an Ansible playbook forked from the Dataverse community’s, and a managed Postgres database, with the 6.x series as the target. That rebuild was not finished where this history stops.


Teaching: The Carpentries and an instructor network
Instruction went through three distinct eras, and the shift between them was reactive, not planned. With two staff and tens of thousands of potential learners, the unit joined The Carpentries in 2017 and used the membership to build an instructor community rather than hire one; Tim founded UCLA Carpentries in 2018 and spent its first two years teaching locally, one campus, in person. Between October 2017 and January 2020 the program ran six Software and Data Carpentry workshops on campus, in R and Python, at the Young Research Library, Powell Library, the IDRE Portal, the Mathematical Sciences building, and the LA Kretz Garden Pavilion for Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, alongside Library Carpentry workshops for librarians and information-studies students in 2017, 2018, and 2019. The instructor rosters show the model working: by the two January 2020 workshops, campus volunteers trained through the program were leading the teaching and DSC staff were mostly helping. COVID changed the economics of that model overnight: travel-based cross-campus training became impossible, but virtual delivery made cross-campus coordination suddenly cheap. Tim co-founded the systemwide UC Carpentries network in 2020 in direct response to that constraint, not as a planned expansion, with Berkeley, San Diego, Santa Barbara, Merced, and Riverside as partner campuses. What followed was sustained, not temporary: the joint series recorded 1,036 attended seats in 2024 and 637 in 2025 across UCLA and partner UC campuses (seats are counted per session, not per person; see the evidence site’s Instruction page for definitions). The unit had gone from teaching its own campus to running system-scale infrastructure other campuses scheduled their own programming around, a change in kind, not just volume.
The Carpentries model mattered as much for who taught as for what was taught. The DSC adopted a Code of Conduct adapted from the Carpentries’ own. Every member of the DSC team trained as a Carpentries instructor, and by 2021 the program had added 13 active instructors, six of them from technical roles elsewhere in the Library: programmers, a digital asset coordinator, a technical product owner. Jamison became a regular lead instructor for the Unix shell in the UC-wide series and wrote a new lesson on Rclone for moving research data. Teaching gave those staff a reason to share what they knew, and gave DSC instructors it could never have hired. Library Carpentry lessons taught librarians and library-school students the same data and coding skills, which made the Library’s public-facing staff better partners on data-heavy research.13
What was taught followed demand. GIS was among the largest categories throughout, and Geography the largest single departmental audience. Qualitative and text-data analysis was a steady line, as were data management plans for the NIH data-sharing policy, high-performance computing, visualization, and 3D data. Machine learning and AI grew from a handful of sessions in 2023.
Tim’s own Carpentries work went past UCLA. An Instructor Trainer since 2016, he received the Carpentries’ Community Service Award in 2018, served on the inaugural Trainers Leadership Committee and co-wrote its bylaws, and edited a full revision of the Instructor Training curriculum. As chair of Library Carpentry’s Curriculum Advisory Committee from 2022 he moved six lessons into the official worldwide curriculum, among them DMP 101, a data management plans lesson aligned to the NIH data-sharing policy. He later co-chaired the Library Carpentry Governance Group, which sets lesson-adoption standards for the global program.


Open science and software curation
The IMLS grant RE-252335-OLS-22 ($237,839, Tim as Project Director)14 treated course material itself as a citable research output: 15 peer-reviewed open-science lessons against 14 proposed, each with a Zenodo DOI, CRediT contributor roles, ORCID identifiers, and Citation File Format metadata, built by 27 authors across 14 teams. Todd Grappone was Co-PI and Zhiyuan Yao, DSC’s spatial data science librarian, coordinated the program; Tim wrote the computational thinking and R lessons and rewrote the Python one. It is the clearest case of the software-curation and open-science strands in this era, and, because a federal award can be checked without anyone’s account of it, the one with the firmest outside evidence.
Tim is also Co-PI on the $1.85M Sloan Foundation grant that established the UC OSPO Network, a six-campus effort to treat open-source software as real scholarly infrastructure. That grant funds the network, not DSC. What DSC got out of it is a local UCLA open-source program office, the lead on the network’s education work, and shared services (licensing guidance, a repository browser, a summer student research program). The need is concrete: a 2025 scan of about 81,000 UC-affiliated code repositories found that 77.5% carried no license at all.
The open-science work also ran through the field’s own organizations. Tim has been a Center for Open Science ambassador since 2016 and taught in the Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the Social Sciences’ Research Transparency and Reproducibility Training, and the Library held a Center for Open Science institutional membership in 2019–20. DSC staff maintain or co-maintain Carpentries lessons taught worldwide, from the Unix shell and R to newer lessons on qualitative data, Wikidata, and using AI coding agents in research without giving up validation and reproducibility.


Spatial data and GIS
Geography has consistently been the unit’s largest single workshop audience. Until the GIS librarian left for a faculty position in August 2024, DSC’s geospatial librarian handled 70 to 80 booked consultations a year, started the systemwide UC GIS Week, ran UC GIS workshops that reached hundreds of people, managed the LARIAC regional aerial-imagery holdings (bought through the archive’s gift fund), and worked with UC San Diego and UC Santa Barbara on geospatial discovery for Dataverse. DSC also ran UCLA’s campus ArcGIS Online platform. It grew to more than 7,000 accounts and over 3,000 active users a year, and since the position went unfilled it has run past its licensed storage with no assigned administrator.15


Emerging technology: 3D capture, drones, and Potree
When the DSC planned its growth in 2018, it named three areas to build toward as it added staff: GIS, augmented and virtual reality, and machine learning.16 The second came through Doug Daniels, whose own career crosses the 2018 line. He joined the Library in 2013 on the help desk, built its first 3D printing service as a technical projects specialist, and from 2016 ran the Lux Lab, the Library’s emerging-technology space for 3D printing and scanning, laser cutting, large-format printing, and VR. In April 2020, after finishing his MLIS, he joined DSC as Emerging Technologies Librarian.17 His first months in the role were the pandemic’s, and the lab’s printers went to producing protective equipment.
The capture work came first. Daniels scanned objects for partners across campus and beyond: Egyptian artifacts at the Getty and the Museo Egizio in Turin with the Cotsen Institute (2018), cuneiform tablets in Library Special Collections, Fowler Museum objects, sarcophagus lids at LACMA, and Scripps’s research vessel FLIP (2021). Medicine became a steady partner: cadaver-arm scans across dissection stages with the Anatomy Lab (2022), now taught in History of Medicine; eye tissue scanned for machine-learning measurement at the Stein Eye Institute; thyroid specimens for Endocrinology (2025); and a 3D-printed surgical probe holder, built with an undergraduate, now in clinical use at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center. The Easter Island Moai scans with Jo Anne Van Tilburg (2022) became a chapter in the Cotsen Institute’s illustrated atlas of the statues.
In 2023 DSC added a field kit: a drone with LiDAR and photogrammetry payloads, an RTK base station for survey-grade positioning, and a dedicated 3D workstation, flown by Daniels under an FAA remote-pilot certificate. It went to Iceland’s Mosfell Valley with a Cotsen doctoral student for a valley-scale survey (one trip, 2024, per Tim 2026-09-02; the Research Enabled by DSC claim register does not yet approve a year, see Open questions), and to ongoing temple mapping at Angkor. At Powell Library, the building named for the family whose gifts funded much of DSC’s growth, the kit flew a drone survey in 2024; an earlier terrestrial LiDAR scan of the building, in 2021, used different equipment.
Capture raised the archive’s oldest question in a new form: once the object is recorded, how does anyone else use it? A point cloud from a survey is usually too large to open as a single file in a browser or to hand out from a download page. DSC’s answer was pointcloud.ucla.edu, a service built on the open-source Potree viewer, which streams large point clouds so they can be explored interactively on the web. Lighter models went to the Lux Lab’s Sketchfab collection. The work stayed tied to standards. Daniels chairs the UC 3D Data Common Knowledge Group (a member from 2020, chair from 2024), which built the ALA-funded 3D Atlas; co-chairs the international IIIF 3D Community Group; and belongs to the IMLS-funded Community Standards for 3D Preservation effort.
Students carried a share of it. The Lux Lab had its own student line until 2024, when its funding became restricted and it merged into DataSquad. The best-known result is the Refugee Material Culture Initiative: with Professor Kelly Nguyen and the Vietnamese Heritage Museum, Daniels 3D scanned the “Boat of Hope,” a river sampan that carried nine refugees out of Vietnam in 1984, and prepared the models for the museum’s public seven-day narrative of one family’s escape; DataSquad student Bianca Badajos helped set up the Potree viewer that hosts it (credit per the Research Enabled by DSC claim register, 2026-09-27). Daniels was named a UCLA Librarian of the Year for 2026, one of two given university-wide by LAUC-LA.18 His work also ran back to the donor relationship: he showed the lab to the Powell Society donor circle at open houses in 2017, 2018, and 2019.


Text, OCR, and machine learning
Machine learning was one of the three areas the DSC planned to grow into in 2018, and it arrived the way most of the unit’s capacity did, through people rather than a new department. Kristian Allen, a Digital Library programmer with a machine-learning background, joined at half time in 2018. Leigh Phan, on the team from 2017, started as a programmer; her early traces in the record are web maps for the archive’s site in 2018. In 2021 her job was rewritten around computational research, with machine learning and AI as its main line, and she became the DSC’s data scientist. A Powell gift paid for a deep-learning workstation in the Young Research Library, the unit’s first local GPU capacity. Phan ran it, loaded it with open-source models researchers could use locally, and when water damage ended the first machine, led the choice of its replacement.19
Text came first as teaching. A line of workshops on qualitative and text data, on cleaning and coding text for qualitative analysis and on open tools for qualitative methods, drew steadily from 2021 on. In consulting it showed up as individual projects: comparing Ming dynasty Buddhist texts with natural-language-processing methods for a graduate student in Asian Languages, or building machine-learning models in R to classify animal behavior from accelerometer data for a doctoral student in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.20 Ethics came along with the methods. Phan and Ibraheem Ali, a sciences data librarian elsewhere in the Library who also taught in the Carpentries program, organized cross-UC data ethics workshops for UC Love Data Week in 2021 and 2022 with colleagues at UC San Diego and UC Berkeley, and published the model.21
OCR is where the archive’s old job met the new tools most directly. A great deal of research evidence sits in scanned images no one can search or count: handwritten tables, printed statistical series, text in scripts ordinary OCR software reads badly. In the unit’s later years Phan led DSC’s work on getting computable text out of them, printed and handwritten alike, and on transcribing recorded speech across languages. The projects came from researchers. For scanned Japanese documents about atomic-bomb survivors, the team compared six tools to find one that could read dense historical Japanese. Handwritten nineteenth-century German tables for a History professor, and handwritten German memoirs for a Sociology professor, defeated standard OCR and needed a different route. The 1976 Iranian National Census sat locked in scanned PDFs. A DataSquad student, Lukas Hager, built the core OCR pipeline those projects shared, and other students containerized a layout-analysis workflow for medieval canon-law texts. By 2026 the team had a triage tool that runs a fast baseline engine and a stronger AI model side by side and recommends the cheapest defensible path to usable text for a given collection. The outputs and research use of each project named here are still being documented.22 The same methods reached audio: transcribing interviews with dance scholars for World Arts and Cultures, and processing recorded conversations for a dissertation in speech research.
The team’s approach to AI followed the archive’s older instincts about stewardship. Where it could, DSC ran open models on its own hardware, so sensitive research material did not leave UCLA and researchers were not tied to a commercial service to read their own sources. AI and machine learning also became a teaching line of its own, growing from a handful of sessions in 2023, and DSC staff published a Carpentries-style lesson on using AI coding agents in research while keeping the work validated and reproducible.
Phan’s later work carried the same habits into research software. After training at the INTERSECT research-software-engineering bootcamp in 2025, she helped write a lesson on building better research software, co-taught a UC Love Data Week 2026 workshop on making research software citable and discoverable (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18615247), and became co-lead of UCLA’s open source program office.


DataSquad: a student research workforce
DataSquad borrowed its model from Carleton College, where a student-staffed data consulting program had been given its own identity and structure.23 UCLA’s version began in 2020 on a Norman Powell gift that paid the first cohort’s salaries and laptops, and became a formal program in 2021 under Tim; Leigh Phan became co-director in 2025. The Library added funds in 2023 to expand the team and add in-person hours. In 2024 it absorbed the Lux Lab student line, and from 2025 a single cohort of six was cross-trained to cover data consulting and 3D work alike.
Students worked with staff, not in front of them, and senior students ran project management. Their share grew as staff capacity shrank. DataSquad students handled 190 of the unit’s scheduled consultations from 2023 to 2025, about a quarter, most of them in 2023. After that their work moved toward sustained project support, where tracked tasks grew from 6 in 2023 to 111 in 2025 (task tracking began in 2023, so part of that rise is record-keeping), as departments started planning research around the team’s availability rather than calling only when something broke. Two long engagements show the kind of work. Lawrence Lee and Madeline Kim rebuilt the pipeline for Carceral Ecologies’ helicopter-surveillance data so that a load that took about 318 minutes ran in about two. Julia Wood, Ethan Allavarpu, Tristan Dewing, and Lee cleaned and restructured the BioCritical Studies Lab’s national deaths-in-custody data, cutting 41,466 records to 29,208 without losing what the lab needed, and built tools the lab could maintain on its own.
It was also a pipeline. DSC documented post-graduation destinations for ten DataSquad students from 2023 to 2025 (a tracked group, not a program-wide rate). All ten went into data or technical roles, with McKinsey, Amazon, AIG, Stanford, and CVS Health among the destinations; Julia Wood joined the Library as a data specialist. The model has been picked up elsewhere through a DataSquad International network and written up in a co-authored chapter in ACRL’s Data Culture. Its research contributions are in the spotlights under Research impact.


People and funding
Much of this era’s expansion ran on Norman Powell’s philanthropy: a data-scientist position, a deep-learning machine and DSC space in the Young Research Library, infrastructure funds that carried Dataverse’s cloud costs for a time, and DataSquad’s seed funding, all separate from his dated $5M December 2016 gift that endowed the University Librarian position.
The people who carried the work were Jamie Jamison (repository and curation), Doug Daniels (3D and emerging technology), Leigh Phan (programmer to data scientist, computational research and AI), Zhiyuan Yao (spatial data science, until 2024), Kristian Allen (software and machine learning, 2018–2024), a data-science facilitator, and the rotating DataSquad students. The full roster, with what is and is not independently documented, is in this companion.

text:
Open discrepancies not yet resolved

1977 is not a founding. Framing mostly settled. Tim, Stephenson’s own Dataverse-page text, and Stiles & Stephenson 2008 all agree: the archive function ran continuously from the 1960s (PBA, then the SRC’s Archive Data Library, “reference-room basis only”); 1977 is when Treiman designed the research-support framework, the unit was named SSDA, and a Data Archivist line and consultative services were added. The sources that “disagree” describe different facets: Stephenson credits Treiman and omits ISSR; the 2017 decks and the OECD directory name ISSR; the published book chapter24 says “part of the Survey Research Center” (which by 1977 was a component of ISSR). Still to check documentarily: whether Treiman’s 1977 framework reported directly to ISSR or to SRC-within-ISSR. Confirm against the 1977–78 UCLA General Catalog.
The 1964 SRC arrangement and Eve Fielder: Stephenson’s Dataverse-page text says the SRC formed in 1964 “under the direction of Eve Fielder” and the PBA merged into its planned Archive Data Library. A published obituary (LA Times, via legacy.com) says Fielder became SRC’s first director only in 1976, that SRC moved in 2004 to a Health Services Research division in UCLA General Internal Medicine, and that she was associate director there until retiring in 2006. Either SRC ran from 1964 under someone else, or the account compresses two events. Not resolved against SRC’s own records.
The ISSR-era director list and three-subperiod structure (spot-verified 2026-09-02): Sears’s ISSR directorship 1993–2008 is independently confirmed (Wikipedia, UCLA psychology page). The three subperiods are grounded in the digitized UCLA General Catalogs (2003–05 through 2013–14). Freeman’s term (1974–1981) and Brewer’s end (1993, when she left for Ohio State and Sears took over) are firm; still open: Brewer’s start year, any gap 1981–1983, and whether the ISSR-to-ISR rename had a formal date/authority (none found).
ISSR-to-ISR rename and ISR dissolution: no date or authority found for either; no director identified for the institute under the ISR name (~2009–2011).
The “8 founding members” of ICPSR, and “through his efforts”: both phrasings are from Stephenson’s Dataverse-page text, the archive’s institutional memory, not an independent record. UCLA’s founding-member status is primary-verified (Miller’s 1962 memo). The “8” is not, Austin’s list has 22, Miller’s 21; “8” may be the “Committee of Eight” (1962–63 correspondence in ICPSR’s Bentley archive), unread. Marvick’s personal founding role is undocumented (see the 1961–1964 section).
UC Carpentries workshop and learner counts: internal summaries give different totals for different scopes (UC Carpentries alone or combined with UCLA Carpentries) and date windows; not yet reconciled. The founding and co-founding dates (UCLA Carpentries 2018, UC Carpentries co-founded 2020) are settled.
Exact dates for three of Norman Powell’s four gifts (data scientist position, deep learning machine/DSC space, DataSquad seed funding). The director’s 2017-2019 program timeline dates two gifts to DSC, December 10, 2018 and December 15, 2019, but does not say which purposes they funded.
Staff dates for 1977-1986, from the repository’s historical database, not yet received.
The Marvick Papers (UCLA Special Collections, 63 boxes, 1955-1998), not yet consulted for primary founding documents, including Marvick’s own 1967 proposal.

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
text:
The history in 30 seconds
UCLA has kept research data for other researchers to use since 1961, when political scientist Dwaine Marvick started the Political Behavior Archive to share survey data on campus. In 1977 the Institute for Social Science Research named that collection the Social Science Data Archive and gave it staff who helped researchers use it. In 2014 the archive moved to the UCLA Library, and in 2018 it became the core of the Library’s Data Science Center, open to every discipline. On August 24, 2026, the Library dissolved the Center as a unit and moved its staff into Research Services.1 The material changed along the way, from punch cards and survey tapes to restricted national datasets, aerial imagery, 3D scans, and scanned pages turned into data. The responsibility for keeping data usable continued: keep that evidence findable, usable, and trustworthy for the next person.

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
text:

Tim Dennis, the author, directed the archive and then the Data Science Center from 2017 through 2026, so the recent chapters are a participant’s account. They are held to cited records where those exist, and the notes say where a claim rests on the author’s own account; the full statement is under The author’s position. title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
section: What persisted, what changed, and why it matters
text:
What persisted, what changed, and why it matters

What persisted: someone answerable for the data
Since 1961 someone at UCLA has been responsible for research data after the study that produced it ended: taking it in, describing it so a stranger could use it, deciding who may see it, and keeping it readable when the technology underneath changed. Five institutional homes held that responsibility in turn: a faculty archive, a survey center, a research institute, a standalone archive in the Social Sciences division, and the Library.
Four kinds of things had to travel with it through each move.

The collections and their documentation. The Los Angeles surveys of the 1970s through the 2000s, with their codebooks (the documentation that says what each question and code means), went from tape to Harvard’s Dataverse and are searchable today through UCLA’s own repository.
The relationships. UCLA was a founding member in 1962 of ICPSR, the national social science data consortium based at the University of Michigan, and the archive still held the ICPSR and Roper Center subscriptions for the campus when it moved to the Library in 2014. Depositors, faculty users, and data vendors dealt with the archive, whatever office it reported to.
The working knowledge. How a dataset was built, what its license allows, what a variable meant in 1974. Much of that lived in people. Jamie Jamison is named in an archive newsletter from about 1979 and still runs the repository.
The obligations. Data-use agreements, preservation commitments, and the 2014 transfer agreement’s provision that if there are substantial changes to the archive’s operations within the Library, the Library and the Social Sciences Division “should meet to discuss and ensure the continuation of College faculty’s access to the services provided by Social Sciences Data Archives.”



What changed: the homes, the users, and above all the material
The archive changed homes four times. It began as a service for social scientists, had become the campus’s de facto data service by the 1990s, and after 2018 served any discipline. The material changed most. Survey files needed codebooks and a reference room. Restricted national data needed a governed computing environment. Point clouds needed a viewer that runs in a browser. Handwritten tables needed OCR before they could be analyzed at all. Each new kind of material asked the same stewardship questions, and the older tools could not answer them.


Why it matters: data stays usable only while someone is accountable for it
A restricted dataset can be used only while its agreement is administered. A repository stays citable only while its identifiers resolve and its software is patched. A scanned collection stays readable only while someone knows how its text was produced. In every transition below, those duties were carried by specific people with specific budgets and systems. Some were nearly dropped: around 1980 the Library declined the 1980 census tapes and the archive took them on, and after 2024 the campus ArcGIS platform was left without an assigned administrator. When stewardship changes hands, the collections, agreements, systems, and working knowledge have to move together. Otherwise the files may survive without the context that made them usable.

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
section: 1961-1964: A political scientist starts a survey data archive
text:
1961-1964: A political scientist starts a survey data archive
Political scientist Dwaine Marvick, who had joined UCLA’s faculty in 1954, founded the Political Behavior Archive (PBA) in 1961.2 Rice and Southall place it in the field’s founding cohort: UCLA’s data service is the fourth-oldest social-science data library in their sample, after the Roper Center (1957), Berkeley (1958), and GESIS (1960), and ahead of ICPSR itself (1962).3 The PBA distributed survey and behavioral data from ICPR (ICPSR’s original name), the Roper Public Opinion Research Center, and local holdings to UCLA researchers.4 A UC memorial calls Marvick “an early advocate and practitioner of computer applications to political data.” No source found so far says why he founded the archive in 1961 in particular, and Heinz Eulau’s detailed 1999 memorial of Marvick never mentions it.5
The next year UCLA was among the founding member institutions of ICPSR. That is confirmed against the primary document: Warren Miller’s August 1962 memo to Rensis Likert lists “University of California at Los Angeles” among the members “as of July 30, 1962.”6 Two details often attached to it are shakier. The archive’s own account says there were eight founding members and that UCLA joined “through [Marvick’s] efforts,” but Miller’s memo lists 21 institutions, and no document found so far gives Marvick a formal role in the founding. His documented ICPSR service begins on its governing board in 1964. The reasoning is in the companion’s open discrepancies.

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
section: 1964-1974: The archive becomes a reference room in a survey center
text:
1964-1974: The archive becomes a reference room in a survey center
The archive’s next home was UCLA’s Survey Research Center (SRC), formed in 1964, which housed an “Archival Data Library” into which the PBA merged.7 Marvick’s August 1967 proposal, “Plans for the Development of a Social Science Archival Data Library in the UCLA Survey Research Center”,8 set out his plan for that library in writing. The proposal is known from Stiles and Stephenson’s citation; the document itself has not turned up yet.
The archive work was already a formal part of the SRC: taking in datasets from the tape-sharing era, keeping their codebooks, and running a reference room where researchers could work out how to use machine-readable data. What did not exist yet was a named unit with its own staff and consulting services. Stiles and Stephenson say the Archival Data Library ran “on a reference-room basis only.” One detail is unresolved: the archive’s own account puts the 1964 SRC “under the direction of Eve Fielder,” but her obituary says she became its first director in 1976.9
The SRC’s main data product in this decade was the Los Angeles Metropolitan Area Surveys (LAMAS): ten waves, 1970–1976, a shared omnibus survey run about twice a year with questions submitted by different researchers.10
The decade’s clearest mark came from outside the archive. Around 1970 the UCLA Library’s Public Affairs Service, under Mary Ryan, bought 1970 census tapes from DUALabs. It was the Library’s first move into numeric data, and it was cited nationally as an early case of a library taking on machine-readable data.11

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
section: 1974-1977: ISSR names the archive and gives it staff
text:
1974-1977: ISSR names the archive and gives it staff
The Institute for Social Science Research (ISSR) was established in 1974 under founding director Howard E. Freeman, a medical sociologist.12 The SRC and its archival data library came under ISSR, but the date of that transfer is not settled: one research pass puts it in 1976 (see the note on the 1977 date below). In 1977 Associate Director Donald Treiman took the library that had run “on a reference-room basis only,” designed a research-support framework for it (working alongside a project across its whole life cycle, still the archive’s stated mission decades later), and formalized it as a named service unit, the Social Science Data Archive (SSDA), with its own Data Archivist line.13 An OECD international directory dates the “ISSR Data Archive at UCLA” to December 1977.14
So 1977 is when the archive was named and staffed, not when it was founded. The work ran without a break through the PBA and the SRC. Sources that seem to disagree about 1977 are describing different parts of the same change; one open question is whether Treiman’s unit reported to ISSR directly or to the SRC within it (see the companion’s open discrepancies).

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
section: 1977-2014: The archive becomes a campus data service
text:
1977-2014: The archive becomes a campus data service
From 1977 to 2014 the archive went through three arrangements.15

ISSR proper, 1977 to the late 2000s. The archive was a service unit of the institute, whose directors were Howard E. Freeman (1974–1981), Marilynn B. Brewer (from about 1983 to 1993), and David O. Sears (1993–2008).
The Institute for Social Research, about 2009 to 2011. The parent was renamed ISR, with the Data Archive still among its components.
A standalone SSDA, about 2011 to 2014, listed on its own as a Social Sciences collection. No source records a formal dissolution of the parent institute, and the reporting line up to the 2014 transfer is unresolved.

Around 1980 the flow ran the other way from the rest of this history. When the UCLA Library decided not to buy the 1980 census tapes, ISSR and SSDA took them on, with the support and storage that came with them.16 Numeric-data stewardship moved from the Library to the archive, the reverse of what would happen in 2014.
The recurring survey work carried on throughout, renamed and reshaped: the Southern California Social Survey (SCSS), then the Los Angeles County Social Survey (LACSS), which ran at least 1992–2002 (series detail in the companion’s 1977–2014 section). By the 1990s the archive had become, in its own staff’s words, “the de facto campus-wide data service unit,” serving public health, education, policy studies, law, and management as well as the social science departments.17 A surviving SSDA newsletter from about 1979 names Martin Pawlocki (programmer), Gina Jamison (the same person as today’s DSC staff member Jina “Jamie” Jamison), and Shirley Lane, who had come from the UCLA Research Library’s machine-readable 1970 Census project.18



Masthead of the archive’s newsletter, about 1979.








Elizabeth Stephenson, then Data Archivist, in the archive’s tape collection. Newsletter caption: “It must be here somewhere.”







Gina (Jamie) Jamison, then Technical Assistant in the Archive. She left for an MFA and later returned; she runs the repository today.





From the archive’s own newsletter, about 1979, as photographed for a 2017 Library staff presentation.
Elizabeth “Libbie” Stephenson is the era’s through-line. ICPSR’s retirement profile dates her UCLA start to about 1977, and she is documented as staff and later Director through the 2014 transfer, retiring in 2016.1920 Her long run of work on bibliographic control, with Sue Dodd’s scholarship, IASSIST, and ICPSR, was early data-citation practice under an older name: making data properly identified and findable. By 2013 SSDA was already testing DDI-Lifecycle, the international standard for describing survey data across its life, and Colectica curation software. The archive also worked across borders on the Intergenerational Stratification and Mobility File, built with Harry Ganzeboom of the Free University in Amsterdam and Donald Treiman, and funded by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research.21

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
section: 2014-2018: The archive moves to the Library and widens its mandate
text:
2014-2018: The archive moves to the Library and widens its mandate
The 2014 transfer agreement (effective 2014, executed 2015) moved SSDA from the Social Sciences Division to the UCLA Library. It carried 2.0 FTE with about $245K in permanent funds covering the two positions’ salary and benefits, plus about $29K in separate permanent funds for subscriptions (ICPSR, Roper, UC Berkeley/SDA, Colectica/Algenta). A separate, small foundation gift fund came too: the Data Archive Purchase Fund (fund no. 604970/56972), set up in the Social Sciences division to support the archive. Elizabeth Stephenson and Jina “Jamie” Jamison came across with it.22 Its stated purpose was to “expand access to the archive’s expertise while modernizing its services.” It also carried a consultation clause: if the Library later made “substantial changes to the operations of Social Sciences Data Archives,” it was to meet with the Social Sciences Division and keep faculty access intact.
In April 2017 Tim Dennis was hired as Director of SSDA, succeeding Stephenson.23 That November he presented “Library Data Archive” to UCLA Library staff, already framing 1961 to 2017 as one arc under the tagline “Providing archive and data services since 1961.”24 The team then reworked the unit’s services through a design-thinking exercise that put “the user as the scholar in need of research support” at the center.25 In spring 2018 the unit was restructured and renamed the Data Science Center (DSC), with a mission written to cover any discipline,

to foster a welcoming research community by developing data literacy and foundational coding skills through consulting and education … supporting researchers throughout the full data life cycle: planning and data management plans; acquisition, storage, cleaning and usage; analysis; publication; curation; and preservation.26

SSDA became a named component of it. Todd Grappone, then the Library’s AUL for Digital Initiatives and IT, handled the 2014 transfer, coined the “Data Science Center” name, and helped design the 2018 service model.27

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
section: 2018–2026: The Data Science Center takes on new kinds of research material
text:
2018–2026: The Data Science Center takes on new kinds of research material
The new name widened the scope; the archive’s work carried on under it. Staff grew from 2.0 FTE (full-time equivalents) at the 2014 transfer to five by about 2021, mostly by redesigning existing Library positions, while the repository, the teaching program, and the kinds of material researchers brought all grew. This chapter follows three changes: the material researchers brought, what DSC built to steward it, and the people and money that kept it running. The author directed the unit throughout, so the chapter rests on cited records; project inventories and career detail are in the companion’s 2018–present detail.

Researchers arrived with material the survey archive was never built for
Survey files still came in. By the early 2020s researchers were also bringing national voter files too large and too restricted to download, drone and aerial imagery, point clouds (millions of measured 3D points that together model an object or a landscape), handwritten tables that no standard text-recognition software could read, and research code with no license. Geography was the largest single departmental audience for DSC workshops from 2020 to April 2024, and DSC ran the campus ArcGIS Online mapping platform, which grew past 7,000 accounts. That ended when the unit’s GIS librarian left for a faculty position in August 2024; the position has not been filled.28
Four cases show how DSC handled that range. Each starts with a stewardship problem and ends with what stayed usable.


The collections kept working, and the curation kept going, under a new name
The legacy SSDA collection lived on Harvard’s hosted Dataverse, a widely used open-source repository for research data, and the archive’s policies, terms, and deposit practice were written for a “Data Archive.” Those policies and deposit procedures stayed in use after the rename. The archive’s policy repository, created in July 2017, was maintained through May 2020, two years after the new name, and in 2018 DSC stood up a UCLA instance of Dataverse. It chose Dataverse for the reasons the archive had chosen it before: support for DDI, the metadata standard for describing survey data; the ability to restrict licensed files; and a range of curation from self-service deposit to fully mediated. DSC connected it to UCLA single sign-on, to DOIs (the persistent identifiers that make a dataset citable), and to preservation through the California Digital Library.29
Rather than migrate the legacy collection immediately, DSC harvested it into the new repository’s search: keep it working first, move it later. Jina “Jamie” Jamison, who came across with the archive in 2014, ran that repository day to day. She wrote the preservation documentation, kept nightly database backups and a tested rebuild script in place, and walked depositors through collections and DOIs.
By 2026 UCLA Dataverse held about 1,390 released datasets: about 376 deposited directly at UCLA and about 1,014 harvested from the legacy SSDA collection. Counting drafts and restricted deposits, the total is about 1,600.30 Reuse is harder to count: some repository records link to related publications, but those links are incomplete and cannot measure total reuse.
The curation continued too, though no longer under the SSDA name. DSC did not publish new studies as the archive; it helped researchers prepare their own data for publication. A two-stage pattern settled in over time. A research group first worked its dataset out and published it in UCLA Dataverse, with DSC helping shape it along the way. Once the data was stable, it could go to ICPSR, which has the staff to curate a dataset down to the level of individual variables and document it for long-term reuse.31 The UCLA Law Behind Bars Data Project, which tracked COVID-19 in prisons, jails, and immigration detention nationally, followed that path: its COVID Prison Policy Index went into UCLA Dataverse in January 2022, and ICPSR released a curated version as study 38730 in 2023. Nicholas Shapiro’s Carceral Ecologies lab did the same with its autopsy analysis of deaths in the Los Angeles County jail: published in UCLA Dataverse in May 2023, released by ICPSR as study 38958 in 2024. DSC consultation records show both projects asking DSC about ICPSR deposit along the way, Carceral Ecologies from 2021 and Behind Bars in 2022. The Williams Institute brought its national surveys of LGBT people, among them TransPop, the first national probability sample of transgender adults in the United States, which reached ICPSR with DSC curation support. Terence Keel’s BioCritical Studies Lab publishes its deaths-in-custody data in UCLA Dataverse, including the autopsy data behind Keel’s book The Coroner’s Silence. It is a candidate for the second stage, made harder because the lab’s data is compiled from many sources.


Restricted voter data got a governed place to be analyzed
Some of the most sought-after data could not be handed out at all. A national voter file, or a dataset that merges records protected under FERPA (student privacy) or HIPAA (health privacy), can be used only inside an environment that enforces who sees what. UCLA’s medical enterprise had that through Mednet, its computing environment, which offered HIPAA-level services such as a HIPAA-compliant Box. The rest of campus had no access to Mednet, and outside the medical enterprise UCLA had no equivalent campus-wide service, though individual departments may have had their own arrangements: no shared, governed way to give a social science student a voter file, and, in the author’s account, no secure place outside medicine to merge restricted data at scale.32
DSC selected and licensed Redivis, a platform for analyzing restricted data in place, took it through UCLA’s security and third-party risk review (protection levels P3 and P4, the two highest in UC’s data classification), negotiated access to the restricted datasets, piloted it in 2022, and launched the governed service in January 2023. It set up 50 seats with data-use-agreement controls, so that routine requests would not wait on one person.33
The main case is the L2 historic voter file, more than 10 TB of national voter history bought through the archive’s gift fund. It arrived as thousands of fragmented state-level files, too large to store locally and too inconsistent to analyze. DSC assembled it into one version-controlled national dataset, published with its own DOI (UCLA Library, L2 Voter History and Demographic Dataset, 2023, doi:10.60603/D37P4R) and presented at FORCE11 2024 by Redivis’s CEO and Graham Straus, the doctoral student who curated it. Straus put the stewardship point plainly: “What happens when I leave UCLA? Will people know how the dataset was constructed? Yes!”



The L2 Voter File’s overview page on UCLA’s Redivis platform, 2024. Description, provenance, and column documentation are open to anyone; the data itself requires an approved access application.


Researchers in several departments use it, on election administration, gentrification, Latino voting, and health and voting. Processing recorded on UCLA’s Redivis platform as a whole grew from 444 GB in its first year to 2.9 PB (petabytes) in 2024. That measures computation across the platform, not storage and not the voter file alone; the data held is about 20 TB. The scholarship belongs to the researchers. DSC supplied the environment, the agreements, and the curated dataset.


OCR turned scanned pages into data
A great deal of research evidence sits in scanned images that no one can search or count: handwritten tables, printed statistical series, text in scripts ordinary OCR (optical character recognition, the software that turns an image of a page into text) reads badly. Getting usable text out of them is the old archival job of making a source accessible, applied to a new kind of source.
The projects came from researchers. For scanned Japanese documents about atomic-bomb survivors, the team compared six tools to find one that could read dense historical Japanese. Handwritten nineteenth-century German tables for a History professor, and handwritten German memoirs for a Sociology professor, defeated standard OCR and needed a different route. The 1976 Iranian National Census sat locked in scanned PDFs. Leigh Phan, DSC’s data scientist, led the work. A DataSquad student, Lukas Hager, built the core pipeline those projects shared. By 2026 the team had a triage tool that runs a fast baseline engine and a stronger AI model side by side and recommends the cheapest defensible route to usable text for a given collection. The outputs and research use of each project above are still being documented.34 Where it could, DSC ran open models on its own hardware, so sensitive material did not leave UCLA and researchers were not tied to a commercial service to read their own sources.


3D capture needed a way for others to open the results
In 2018 DSC named three areas to grow into as it added staff: GIS, augmented and virtual reality, and machine learning.35 The second came through Doug Daniels, who had joined the Library in 2013 on the help desk, built its first 3D printing service, and from 2016 ran the Lux Lab, the Library’s space for 3D printing, scanning, and VR. He joined DSC as Emerging Technologies Librarian in April 2020.36 He scanned objects for partners across campus and beyond, from Egyptian artifacts at the Getty and the Museo Egizio in Turin with the Cotsen Institute to cadaver-arm dissections for the Anatomy Lab, now taught in History of Medicine, and in 2023 DSC added a drone kit with LiDAR (laser-ranging) and photogrammetry payloads for landscape-scale surveys.
Capture made a new stewardship problem. A point cloud from a survey is usually too large to open as a single file in a browser or to hand out from a download page. DSC’s answer was pointcloud.ucla.edu, a server Daniels built in 2022 on the open-source Potree viewer, which streams large point clouds so anyone can explore them in an ordinary web browser.
One publicly documented result is the Refugee Material Culture Initiative. With Classics professor Kelly Nguyen and the Vietnamese Heritage Museum, Daniels 3D scanned the “Boat of Hope,” a six-meter river sampan that carried nine refugees out of Vietnam in 1984, and prepared the models for the museum’s digital exhibit, a public seven-day narrative of one family’s escape by sea. DataSquad student Bianca Badajos helped set up the Potree viewer that hosts it.



The “Boat of Hope” seven-day narrative in DSC’s Potree viewer on pointcloud.ucla.edu. Model, story, and the survivors’ photograph (inset): Refugee Material Culture Initiative and the Vietnamese Heritage Museum. Explore it in 3D.


Daniels was named a UCLA Librarian of the Year for 2026, one of two given university-wide by LAUC-LA.37 His standards work, chairing the UC 3D Data Common Knowledge Group and co-chairing the international IIIF 3D Community Group, tied the service to how other institutions preserve 3D data. The full project list is in the companion’s Daniels inventory.


Teaching spread the skills further than a small staff could reach
With two staff and tens of thousands of potential learners, the unit joined The Carpentries in 2017, a nonprofit that trains volunteer instructors to teach foundational coding and data skills, and used the membership to build an instructor community rather than hire one. Tim founded UCLA Carpentries in 2018. By the two January 2020 workshops, campus volunteers trained through the program were leading the teaching and DSC staff were mostly helping. COVID then made in-person cross-campus training impossible and virtual coordination cheap, and in 2020 Tim co-founded the systemwide UC Carpentries network with Berkeley, San Diego, Santa Barbara, Merced, and Riverside. The joint series recorded 1,036 attended seats in 2024 and 637 in 2025 across UCLA and partner campuses (seats are counted per session, not per person; definitions are on the evidence site’s Instruction page).
Every member of the DSC team trained as a Carpentries instructor, and by 2021 six of the program’s 13 new instructors came from technical roles elsewhere in the Library. Teaching gave those staff a reason to share what they knew, and gave DSC instructors it could never have hired.38 GIS was among the largest topics throughout; qualitative and text data, data management plans, and later machine learning followed demand.
Consulting widened the same way. From 2023 through 2025 DSC recorded 785 scheduled consultations, 156 service-desk tickets, and 234 tracked project tasks. The categories describe different kinds of work and should be read separately. Over those years the work shifted from single appointments toward project support that ran for months.39 An IMLS grant (RE-252335-OLS-22, $237,839, Tim as Project Director)40 treated course material as a citable research output: 15 peer-reviewed open-science lessons, each with a DOI and contributor credits, built by 27 authors. Tim’s own Carpentries, open-science, and open-source leadership is in the companion’s 2018–present detail.


Staff never grew in proportion; students and redesigned jobs filled the gap
Between January 2020 and February 2026, datasets deposited directly in UCLA Dataverse went from 9 to about 376. Staff grew far less, and mostly from redesigning existing Library positions: a geospatial librarian rebuilt as a Spatial Data Science Librarian (Zhiyuan Yao), a Library IT data manager rebuilt as a Data Science Facilitator, and a Digital Library programmer with a machine-learning background recruited across divisions at half time (Kristian Allen, 2018–2024).41 Some capacity was simply lost: when the GIS librarian left for a faculty position in August 2024, the position went unfilled, with the demand still there.
Students made up much of the difference. DataSquad borrowed its model from a student-staffed data consulting program at Carleton College.42 UCLA’s version began in 2020 on a Norman Powell gift, became a formal program in 2021, and in 2024 absorbed the Lux Lab’s student line. Students handled 190 of the unit’s scheduled consultations from 2023 to 2025, about a quarter, then moved toward long project work. For Carceral Ecologies, Nicholas Shapiro’s lab, Lawrence Lee and Madeline Kim rebuilt the pipeline for helicopter-surveillance flight data so that one measured data-loading step that had taken about 318 minutes ran in about two. For Terence Keel’s BioCritical Studies Lab, Julia Wood, Ethan Allavarpu, Tristan Dewing, and Lee cleaned and restructured a national deaths-in-custody dataset and built tools the lab could maintain on its own.



The 2024–25 DataSquad cohort at the Data Science Center, from the DataSquad site’s November 2024 introduction.


DSC documented post-graduation destinations for ten DataSquad students from 2023 to 2025. All ten entered data or technical roles. This is a tracked group, not an outcome rate for every student in the program.
Norman Powell’s philanthropy paid for much of the expansion: a data-scientist position, a deep-learning workstation and DSC space in the Young Research Library, about two years of AWS costs after DSC got its own AWS account, and DataSquad’s seed funding, all separate from his December 2016 gift endowing the University Librarian position. The people who carried the work were Jamie Jamison (repository and curation), Doug Daniels (3D and emerging technology), Leigh Phan (programmer, then data scientist), Zhiyuan Yao (spatial data science, until 2024), Kristian Allen (software and machine learning, 2018–2024), a data-science facilitator, and the rotating DataSquad students. The full roster is in the companion.



Data Science Center staff, 2024, from the DataSquad site’s November 2024 introduction.




Paying for the systems, and for the data
The repository and several shared platforms relied on cloud services. UCLA Dataverse runs on Amazon Web Services, with about 5.4 TiB of files, counting replication, as of May 2025; the point-cloud service has its own AWS server; Redivis is licensed. Dataverse first ran under the Library IT division’s AWS account. When campus broke up its shared AWS arrangement and DSC got its own account, the cost landed on DSC. Powell infrastructure funds covered it for about two years, and after that it came out of the archive’s operating fund.
That operating fund, the one the 2014 transfer set up, paid the recurring costs: the ICPSR and Roper memberships, AWS, and Redivis, which University Librarian discretionary funds had backed for its first two years. Those costs grew. ICPSR and Roper moved to higher pricing tiers, and cloud costs rose with the repository; two small subscriptions, SDA and Colectica, were dropped along the way. The Library added money to the fund over time to cover the difference, and that is a large part of how the Library paid for DSC’s growth.
The gift fund did a different job. The Data Archive Purchase Fund bought data for UCLA researchers: the L2 national voter file, the LARIAC aerial imagery, and four large English corpora (the Corpus of Contemporary American English, the Corpus of Historical American English, News on the Web, and the Coronavirus Corpus), which sit in UCLA Dataverse under a license that limits them to UCLA faculty and graduate students.43 By 2025 DSC had also begun rebuilding the Dataverse service as code, so it could be recreated and upgraded; that rebuild was not finished where this history stops.


August 2026: the unit is dissolved
On August 24, 2026, the Library dissolved the Data Science Center as a unit and moved its staff into Research Services. The Library says “the expertise available and services offered remain the same” and that services will be evaluated through the coming year. It has announced two changes: drone lending ends in fall 2026, and DataSquad will no longer run as a coordinated program.44 On October 5, 2026, the Library posted a new Mercator Geospatial Information and Maps Librarian position. This history stops at that point and does not assess the Library’s restructure proposal, which its author has not seen.

Los Angeles Metropolitan Area Surveys (LAMAS), 1970–1976, ten waves
Edward Bixler and colleagues’ 1979 study of sleep disorders, using five sleep questions added to the 1973 wave, regarded as the first rigorous study in sleep epidemiology45


Southern California Social Survey (SCSS), through 1991
Christof Nägel and Amy Nivette’s 2023 reanalysis of 1991 and 1992 survey data on confidence in the police; the 1991 survey is preserved on Harvard Dataverse46


Los Angeles County Social Survey (LACSS), 1992–2002
Gershon and Pantoja’s 2011 study of English-only attitudes, pooling the 1997 and 1998 waves; Zambrana and colleagues’ 2021 review of Latina/o data sets; Gutierrez’s 2025 study of group consciousness in California47



Where these surveys can be traced, they were still being used decades later, in work on sleep, racial attitudes, language policy, and policing. A search of ICPSR’s Bibliography of Data-related Literature, by study number, on August 9, 2026 found three publications for LACSS and none for LAMAS, and SCSS is not in that index. That search understates use. Absence from an index does not mean a series went unused, especially for surveys from the 1970s, which predate modern data-citation norms. The search method is in the companion’s chart methods.

title: From the Political Behavior Archive to the Data Science Center
text:
Methods and limitations

The author’s position
Tim Dennis directed the Social Science Data Archive and the Data Science Center from April 2017 through 2026. This is his account of the archive’s history, written to leave a record of work that ran for six decades and was reorganized out of its standalone form on August 24, 2026. It is a point of view. The record it rests on is held to a plain standard:

Claims about the recent decades are tied to cited institutional records wherever those exist. Where a claim rests on the author’s own account as director, the note says so. Because the author took part in those years, they are held to a higher documentation standard than the earlier ones, not a looser one.
Judgments about what worked and what was lost are marked as judgments.
Claims about cause are kept within what the evidence supports.
Work done by a team is credited to the team. Individuals are named where authorship, formal authority, or accountability makes it matter.

Evidence cutoff: 2026-08-31 for the period covered. Corrections and first-hand accounts were added through 2026-09-29. The working evidence files and version history are kept in a private repository. To report an error or add context, use the correction link at the foot of each page.


How the evidence is handled
The author also wrote documents, including a grant proposal and material responding to the reorganization, that use some of the same facts to make a case. This history keeps the two apart in these ways:

The author’s role is stated plainly, here and at the top, rather than left for the reader to find.
Facts are checked against a private register of claims that records what is verified, disputed, or self-reported. Documents that cite this history are not independent corroboration of claims that trace back to the same author.
Documented facts are kept separate from interpretation. Discontinuities, gaps, and contested points are stated as such rather than smoothed over; see the companion’s open discrepancies and open questions.
Some 2018-present detail was first found in internal review documents. Those are used to find facts, not as sole public evidence: a claim appears only where independent corroboration exists (press coverage, award records, publication venues, grant award pages) or where it is marked as self-reported.
Contemporary impact claims follow the Research Enabled by DSC site’s claim register, which records the approved wording and what is not approved for each case.



Where the full record is
The companion holds the full roster, the 1977–2014 detail, the 2018–present detail, the Daniels project inventory, the Powell gifts, the chart methods, the open discrepancies, and the open questions.
